title: Frank Reynolds' Little Beauties

jokes.text: Characters debating whether America had kings, then someone immediately breaks their nose walking into something
jokes.setup: Mundane, oddly confident argument about whether America ever had kings — a strangely stupid debate delivered with conviction
jokes.punchline: Mid-argument, someone walks into something and breaks their nose, cutting the debate cold with 'Son of a bitch!'
jokes.explanation: Classic cold open chaos — the stupidity of the argument is funny on its own (confident wrongness), but the physical interruption pays it off with a sharp economy. The transition into the main plot is abrupt and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Son of a bitch!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Guys, guys, guys.
Oh.
Are you okay?
Oh!
I think you broke your nose.

jokes.text: 'You met a strange man at a titty bar who offered you a great opportunity to invest in a beauty pageant? Everything looked very legit.'
jokes.setup: Frank excitedly pitches his investment in a beauty pageant he heard about from a stranger at a strip club
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly summarizes the entire scam-tier scheme back to Frank and Frank confirms with 'Everything looked very legit'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's deadpan recap of the scheme's absurdity is a perfect straight-man moment, and Frank's breezy confirmation ('Everything looked very legit') is excellent character comedy — his complete lack of self-awareness is exactly on-brand. The structure is clean: build up, flat recap, oblivious confirmation.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, strange man, titty bar.

jokes.text: 'Because you make a lot of cash, and you ogle some broads.' / 'Yeah, I don't question that aspect of it.'
jokes.setup: Frank is asked why he'd ever want to run a beauty pageant
jokes.punchline: Frank's honest answer is pure mercenary/pervy reasoning, and Mac responds not with shock but with casual agreement — 'seems right up your alley, bro'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Mac's total lack of moral objection — the normalization of Frank's crudeness by the gang is a reliable Always Sunny engine. Not exceptional but efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Because you make a lot of cash, and you ogle some broads.

jokes.text: Frank explains the other organizer 'got pinched for coming on to one of the contestants' and now Frank is implicated
jokes.setup: Frank is explaining why he's in trouble with his pageant investment
jokes.punchline: The reveal that his business partner was a predator caught in the act, and Frank is now 'lumped in with a diddler'
jokes.explanation: The word 'diddler' is a signature Always Sunny euphemism that lands — dark subject handled with a deliberately crude diminutive. Sets the thematic engine of the episode.

dialogue.line: Oh! Looks like somebody forgot their swimsuit.

jokes.text: 'Any second now, there's gonna be broads walking through that door in swimsuits.' / 'Awesome.' / 'Yeah, I don't see what the problem is here, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank warns them something bad is about to happen — women in swimsuits are about to walk in
jokes.punchline: The gang responds with enthusiastic approval, completely missing that the problem is coming
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup — Frank treats the swimsuit contestants as a problem, the gang treats it as a gift. The punchline arrives visually when children walk in. Great three-beat structure: Frank's dread, the gang's delight, the reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's the problem.

jokes.text: Children in swimsuits walk through the door — 'That's the problem.'
jokes.setup: Gang eagerly anticipates attractive women in swimsuits
jokes.punchline: Small children parade in instead, with Frank delivering the flat payoff: 'That's the problem.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect visual punchline. The economy is exceptional — 'That's the problem.' does enormous work in three words after a full scene of buildup. The gap between the gang's excitement and the reality is the whole joke, and it lands hard. One of the best-structured moments in the episode. Earns high marks for structure and economy.

dialogue.line: How would you win pageants? Did you have a different face?

jokes.text: Dee mentions she did pageants as a kid; Dennis immediately says their mom told her not to bother because 'she isn't pretty enough'
jokes.setup: Dee claims she willingly entered pageants as a kid, defending the practice
jokes.punchline: Dennis casually reveals their mother actively told Dee she wasn't pretty enough to bother — delivered with no emotional weight
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny dynamic — the gang's casual cruelty toward Dee is a running engine and Dennis's flat delivery of their mother's childhood abuse lands as dark comedy. Character-specific: only Dennis delivers trauma this blandly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, she was a dog back then, too.

jokes.text: 'How would you win pageants? Did you have a different face?' / 'No, she was a dog back then, too.'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to defend her pageant-winning past as evidence she was attractive
jokes.punchline: Dennis questions how she could have won given her current appearance; Frank confirms she was equally unattractive as a child
jokes.explanation: 'Did you have a different face?' is a sharp, specific insult that earns its cruelty through wit. The follow-up 'she was a dog back then, too' is cruder but efficient. The two-step delivery gives it rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: In other countries, okay, women that can't show their ankles, right? They got to be in those big, black tarps or whatever. In America, we can show toddlers in tiny bikinis

jokes.text: Frank's speech comparing women in countries who 'can't show their ankles' in 'big black tarps' to American toddlers in tiny bikinis — framed as a freedom argument
jokes.setup: Frank tries to defend child beauty pageants as an American tradition worth protecting
jokes.punchline: He constructs a deranged 'freedom' comparison between Islamic modesty culture and hypersexualizing toddlers — presented with sincere patriotic pride
jokes.explanation: Frank deploying a warped 'freedom' logic to justify something deeply questionable is peak Always Sunny — the joke is that his reasoning is internally consistent but arrives somewhere monstrous. 'Big black tarps' as the contrast point is deliriously crude. The character specificity is high: this speech could only come from Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We can do whatever we want with our kids. And that's what America is all about.

jokes.text: Charlie's inspirational conclusion: 'We should dress up our little kids just to show other people that we can.' / 'You just loaded up that train with coal!'
jokes.setup: Frank's deranged freedom argument is building toward some kind of rallying cry
jokes.punchline: Charlie synthesizes it into the most vapid, creepy 'inspirational' statement possible, and Frank responds with genuine enthusiasm ('That was inspiring as hell')
jokes.explanation: The 'train loaded with coal' metaphor applied to Charlie's profoundly dumb inspirational thought is a great absurdist beat. Frank's sincerity in praising it makes it funnier. Escalates naturally out of the previous speech.

dialogue.line: U.S.A. U.S.A., U.S.A., U.S.A., U.S.A., U.S.A.!

jokes.text: USA chant erupts in the bar over a child beauty pageant
jokes.setup: The gang has just talked themselves into hosting a child pageant using patriotism as justification
jokes.punchline: They break into a full USA chant, treating this grotesque undertaking like a sports victory
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation cap on the speech sequence. Not particularly original — USA chants as ironic punctuation are a common move — but it fits the moment and gets a solid communal laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I am not gonna diddle your kids. I'm not like that. That's not my thing. I met that guy in a titty bar.

jokes.text: Frank's opening remarks to the parents: 'I am not gonna diddle your kids. I'm not like that. That's not my thing. I met that guy in a titty bar.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to reassure nervous parents by distancing himself from his disgraced former partner
jokes.punchline: His reassurance consists entirely of explicit denial of child abuse and a reference to meeting his partner at a strip club — the worst possible optics delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is a standout moment. The joke structure is impeccable: the more Frank tries to defend himself, the more damning his words become. 'I am not gonna diddle your kids' as an opening statement to parents is precisely calibrated cringe — the specificity of the denial makes it worse. 'I met that guy in a titty bar' as his exculpatory evidence is a perfect kicker. Pure Always Sunny DNA.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Do I look suspicious?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You look grotesque.

jokes.text: Frank's bloody nose during the opening speech — 'Do I look suspicious?' / 'You look grotesque.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to appear legitimate and reassuring to the parents while his face is a bloody mess
jokes.punchline: He asks if he looks suspicious (a legitimacy question); Dee sidesteps the question entirely to note he looks grotesque (a different problem entirely)
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'suspicious' to 'grotesque' is a clean misdirection — Frank is worried about the wrong problem entirely. Dee's answer is perfectly calibrated: not reassuring, but also not the concern Frank had. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We got to definitely write a song about how we do not diddle kids.

jokes.text: Mac spontaneously sings a rough draft anti-diddling song: '♪ Do not diddle kids, it's no good diddling kids ♪'
jokes.setup: The gang decides they need to prove their innocence at the pageant
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution is to write a song literally about not diddling kids — the most counterproductive PR move imaginable
jokes.explanation: The absurdist logic — writing a song about not doing something to prove you don't do it — is a great comedic concept, and hearing the words sung earnestly amplifies it. The immediate counter-observation ('there is no quicker way for people to think you are diddling kids') makes the punchline land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: There is no quicker way for people to think that you are diddling kids than by writing a song about it.

jokes.text: 'There is no quicker way for people to think that you are diddling kids than by writing a song about it.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just enthusiastically pitched a song explicitly about not abusing children as their PR strategy
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the obvious-but-perfectly-phrased counter-logic with flat certainty
jokes.explanation: A great straight-man line that works as the punchline to Mac's absurdism. The phrasing is quotable and precise. Dennis's certainty ('no quicker way') gives it authority. Would rank higher if it weren't reactive — it's a great response but not a fully constructed joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: But there's a guy. Uh, uh, there's a fat guy. Well, his face is busted to bits, and he... he's in charge. Real jacked up face and fat.

jokes.text: Frank attempts his own anti-diddling song: '♪ I wouldn't do it with anybody younger than my daughter, and no little kids ♪'
jokes.setup: Despite Dennis's warning that writing such a song would backfire, Frank immediately tries to write one anyway
jokes.punchline: Frank's lyric compares acceptable partners to his own daughter's age, which is somehow worse than what he's trying to refute
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation — Frank heard Dennis's warning and ignored it, then made his version worse by using his daughter as a benchmark. The escalation from bad idea to worse execution is a strong Always Sunny beat. Character-specific: only Frank would choose this reference point.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, those mothers just left their kids here in a bar with complete strangers in a pageant that's under investigation. They're terrible parents.

jokes.text: Charlie's response to being asked who's in charge: 'Well, usually that's whoever yells the loudest, but I am the only one here right now, so I am in charge.'
jokes.setup: Walter (the inspector) arrives and asks who's in charge
jokes.punchline: Charlie describes the gang's actual chaotic power structure with complete honesty, then claims authority by default
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever piece of character writing — Charlie accidentally reveals everything true about the gang's dysfunction while trying to answer a simple question. 'Whoever yells the loudest' is both a great joke and a perfect description of the show's actual power dynamics. High character integration: this is quintessential Charlie obliviousness-as-honesty.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I see amateurs, I see trash, little pieces of trash on my stage. You guys are dummies.

jokes.text: Walter Harris from the 'Family Association for the Protection of Children' introduces himself — Charlie panics: 'Oh! Okay. Uh, you know, I'm pretty much... I'm in charge of this... the chairs.'
jokes.setup: An inspector from a child protection organization arrives
jokes.punchline: Charlie's panic causes him to immediately demote himself to 'in charge of... the chairs' — a spectacularly unconvincing deflection
jokes.explanation: The specific nature of Charlie's self-demotion ('the chairs') is funny — he doesn't just say 'I'm nobody,' he assigns himself the most specific and mundane possible responsibility. The panic-induced specificity is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Samantha gets to be mean because Samantha is a star, okay? Maybe one day you'll be a star, but right now you're not. You're junk.

jokes.text: Charlie panics and describes Frank to Walter to redirect him: 'There's a fat guy. His face is busted to bits, and he's in charge.'
jokes.setup: Charlie realizes he doesn't want to deal with the inspector and tries to redirect him to Frank
jokes.punchline: His description of Frank — 'fat guy, face is busted to bits' — is both accurate and absurdly unflattering as a way to identify someone
jokes.explanation: Charlie's physical description of Frank is funny primarily because of its bluntness and accuracy — 'face is busted to bits' is a vivid, undignified descriptor. His cowardly deflection is on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You belong in the bathroom. Go!

jokes.text: 'Those mothers just left their kids here in a bar with complete strangers in a pageant that's under investigation. They're terrible parents.'
jokes.setup: Mac is saying they should welcome the inspector because they have nothing to hide
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to condemning the parents for leaving kids with the gang — oblivious to the hypocrisy
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny — the gang criticizing others for behavior that is objectively less bad than their own. Mac condemning the parents for leaving kids with strangers, while he is the stranger and the event is under investigation, is a solid irony beat.

dialogue.speaker: Samantha
dialogue.line: You're ugly.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You don't-- that's not something you say. You're mean. You're the meanest girl in the world.

jokes.text: Gang immediately reveals they pinned the whole thing on Frank behind his back after spending a scene comforting him
jokes.setup: The gang spends a whole exchange assuring Frank everything will be fine and they'll handle it
jokes.punchline: The moment Frank leaves, Mac asks 'You pinned the whole thing on him, right?' and gets an immediate 'Of course I did'
jokes.explanation: The speed of the betrayal — the instant Frank exits — is the joke. It's compressed and efficient. The characters' awfulness is the entire engine, and this is a clean, well-timed expression of it. The 'of course I did' removes any doubt about the gang's moral calculus.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: All hair is technically dead, you stupid idiot smarty-pants stupid, stupid idiot.

jokes.text: Dee screaming at the children on stage: 'I see amateurs, I see trash, little pieces of trash on my stage.'
jokes.setup: Dee is running pageant rehearsal and styling herself as a tough director
jokes.punchline: She calls literal children 'trash' and 'little pieces of trash' with the energy of a Broadway tyrant
jokes.explanation: Dee abusing small children with the vocabulary of a fired-up stage director is a solid cringe gag. The specificity of 'little pieces of trash' — the word 'little' — adds an extra cruel detail. Her deluded sense of authority is on-brand.

dialogue.line: Terrible breath. Wheezing.

jokes.text: 'Samantha's mean.' / 'Samantha gets to be mean because Samantha is a star. Maybe one day you'll be a star, but right now you're not. You're junk.'
jokes.setup: A child complains that the star contestant, Samantha, is mean
jokes.punchline: Dee defends Samantha's cruelty with star-entitlement logic, then tells the child they are 'junk'
jokes.explanation: The 'you're junk' landing is sharp — Dee's conditional empathy followed by a direct insult to a child is both cruel and perfectly in character. The star-privilege argument applied to children is a great escalation of absurd logic.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: This is what America is about, okay, being able to eat at any rate you want to eat.

jokes.text: 'I have to go to the bathroom.' / 'You belong in the bathroom. Go!'
jokes.setup: A child interrupts Dee's breakdown to say they need the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Dee repurposes it as an insult — 'you belong in the bathroom'
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient line with surprising snap. Dee repurposing a mundane request as a withering dismissal is a good bit of comedy economy. The speed of the comeback is the main value.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Your mom doesn't know dick. She's a dumb, fat cow, and your sister-- she is a stupid little shit-mouthed bitch, isn't she?

jokes.text: Dee approaches Samantha to bond with her; Samantha says 'You're ugly' mid-compliment
jokes.setup: Dee sees herself in the mean, competitive child and approaches her as a potential kindred spirit
jokes.punchline: Samantha calls her ugly mid-attempt at connection — the child is more ruthless than the adult
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Dee, who was just calling children 'trash' and 'junk,' gets out-brutaled by an actual child. The child is more naturally vicious than Dee can be. Good character work: Dee's delusion about being a star is punctured by someone who doesn't respect her performance of authority.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I know, but it's not what you care about, it's what I care about.

jokes.text: 'All hair is technically dead, you stupid idiot smarty-pants stupid, stupid idiot. You better watch yourself, Samantha.'
jokes.setup: Samantha says Dee's hair 'looks dead'; Dee tries to come back with a scientific rebuttal
jokes.punchline: The scientific rebuttal devolves instantly into 'stupid idiot smarty-pants stupid, stupid idiot' — Dee loses the insult battle to a child
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier lines in the episode. The escalation from 'all hair is technically dead' (a real attempt at a comeback) to 'stupid idiot smarty-pants stupid, stupid idiot' is perfectly observed — Dee starts smart and immediately collapses into child-level insults. The repetition of 'stupid' and 'idiot' shows her losing the thread in real time. High character integration: this is exactly how Dee's confidence unravels.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I had it done at a funeral home. Where in the hell am I going to go-- to the goddamn makeup counter at Macy's? You go to a funeral home to get gruesome repairs.

jokes.text: Samantha's comeback to Dee's threat: 'Knock, knock.' / 'Who's there?' / 'Terrible breath.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just threatened Samantha and is trying to regain authority
jokes.punchline: Samantha defuses the entire power dynamic by pivoting to a knock-knock joke that's just a personal insult
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and structure. The knock-knock format creates a brief moment where Dee has to play along (she can't refuse 'who's there' without looking stupid), and then 'terrible breath' as the punchline is both devastatingly simple and perfectly targeted. It's also an amazing character beat — Samantha is too young for elaborate insults so she uses a child's format, which makes it more humiliating. Near-perfect setup/subversion.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You look like you're at your own wake.

jokes.text: Frank wheezing and eating simultaneously while trying to make an America argument
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to make a point about America while visibly struggling to breathe and eat at the same time
jokes.punchline: Dennis: 'Breathe and eat separately.' Frank insists this, too, is about America
jokes.explanation: 'Breathe and eat separately' is a funny line; Dennis's weary pragmatism contrasting with Frank's wheezing patriotism is a solid physical/verbal combo. The 'this is what America is about' callback to the earlier freedom argument is a good running gag extension.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Go into the toilet and run your mouth under the sink.

jokes.text: 'This is what America is about, okay, being able to eat at any rate you want to eat.'
jokes.setup: Frank is wheezing while eating; Dennis tells him to separate the two
jokes.punchline: Frank turns his eating disorder into a freedom argument — a callback to Charlie's 'America' speech from earlier
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — the 'America means we can do anything' logic from Charlie's speech is now being applied to Frank's physical deterioration. The escalating wrongness of things being framed as American freedom is a consistent comedic thread.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I figure he's a cretin. Why would I have a cretin like that near me if I have something to hide?

jokes.text: Mac's explanation for why a boy is in the pageant: 'Dad probably skipped town. Mom always wanted a daughter, so she sticks her little boy in the pageant to play out her little fantasies.'
jokes.setup: The gang notices a boy competing in the girls' pageant
jokes.punchline: Mac's instant psychological backstory for the child is both dark and stated with zero emotion, as if it's obvious
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny for the confidence and speed of the armchair psychology, but the punchline is immediately undercut by the reveal that the boy actually loves pageants. Functions as setup more than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Which one of these talented, uh, entertainers, who I am not attracted to at all, will be the winner? I'm not attracted to any of them, none of them.

jokes.text: Benjamin spontaneously breaks into Yankee Doodle Dandy — the boy genuinely loves pageantry
jokes.setup: Mac has just confidently explained that the boy is being pushed into pageantry against his will
jokes.punchline: Benjamin launches into a full enthusiastic song, completely disproving Mac's theory — 'I don't think this boy is being pushed into this at all'
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of Mac's confident psych analysis. The visual of a small boy launching into Yankee Doodle Dandy with full gusto while the gang watches is a great misdirection payoff. The understated 'I don't think this boy is being pushed' follow-up lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Justine
dialogue.line: A big, humungous pain in my Vagina...

jokes.text: Dennis motivates Justine: 'Your mom doesn't know dick. She's a dumb, fat cow, and your sister — she is a stupid little shit-mouthed bitch, isn't she?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to inspire Justine, a girl whose mother said she isn't pretty enough to win
jokes.punchline: His motivational speech consists entirely of explicit insults about her family, delivered to her face with the warmth of a life coach
jokes.explanation: Dennis's motivational coaching being indistinguishable from abuse is a great character moment. The specificity of 'shit-mouthed bitch' applied to a sibling he's never met is bold. The girl's flat reaction ('you just said a lot of bad words') is the perfect deadpan counter. High character integration: Dennis's condescension and self-delusion as a mentor is consistent with his psychology.

dialogue.line: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall. The only thing we have to fear is... fear itself.

jokes.text: Justine's reaction: 'You just said a lot of bad words.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered a string of explicit insults about Justine's family as 'motivation'
jokes.punchline: The child's response is a flat, non-emotional factual observation — 'you just said a lot of bad words'
jokes.explanation: Perfect reaction beat. The understatement is calibrated precisely — she doesn't cry, doesn't get angry, just calmly notes the linguistic facts. The economy is near-perfect: nine words do everything needed. Pairs beautifully with Dennis's oblivious response ('it's not what you care about, it's what I care about').

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You bang the dead bodies? I don't give a shit. If I was dead, you could bang me all you want. Who cares? Dead body's like a piece of trash.

jokes.text: 'I know, but it's not what you care about, it's what I care about.'
jokes.setup: Justine says she doesn't really care about winning the pageant
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses her indifference by clarifying that her participation is entirely for his benefit, not hers
jokes.explanation: One of the best character lines in the episode. Dennis's narcissism is so complete that he openly admits to a child that he's using her emotional journey as a vehicle for his own feelings. 'It's not what you care about, it's what I care about' is a perfect distillation of Dennis Reynolds as a person. High quotability, high character integration — this only works coming from Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Fill me up with cream. Make a stew out of my ass. What's the big deal? Bang me, eat me, grind me up into little pieces, throw me in the river.

jokes.text: Frank has gone to a funeral home to fix his broken nose — 'I had it done at a funeral home.'
jokes.setup: Frank returns and his face looks horrifying despite having been 'fixed'
jokes.punchline: He explains he went to a funeral home for cosmetic repair — his logic being there's nowhere else to go for a 'gruesome repair'
jokes.explanation: Frank's skewed logic — 'where else are you gonna go for gruesome repairs?' — is excellent character comedy. The idea of a funeral home as the natural choice for facial reconstruction is both absurd and consistent with Frank's worldview. The payoff line 'you look like you're at your own wake' is a good kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That was a mistake. The janitor got a hold of the P.A. system. Puerto Rican guy.

jokes.text: 'You look like you're at your own wake.'
jokes.setup: Frank's funeral-home-repaired face is apparently ghastly
jokes.punchline: Mac's description — 'you look like you're at your own wake' — is a vivid, perfectly chosen image
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economic image. 'At your own wake' perfectly captures the horror of mortician makeup on a living person. It's a good joke with high economy but slightly low character integration — most people could deliver this line.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Man's a diddler. Sick son of a bitch goes around all these kids pageants, pretends he's an inspector. We've been looking for him for a while.

jokes.text: Frank asks for water because his mouth is dry; Dennis tells him to 'run your mouth under the sink' in the toilet
jokes.setup: Frank complains his mouth is dry and needs water
jokes.punchline: Dennis's solution is for Frank to crouch over a bathroom sink and run water into his mouth like an animal
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating Frank with contempt dressed as a practical solution is a reliable dynamic. The specific image of Frank lapping water from a bathroom sink is funny but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: So, there's another unrelated diddler in the mix?

jokes.text: Frank invites the mortician to the event: 'I figure he's a cretin. Why would I have a cretin like that near me if I had something to hide?'
jokes.setup: Frank is accused of making things worse by associating with a mortician
jokes.punchline: Frank's alibi logic: surrounding yourself with a cretin proves innocence because a guilty man would avoid cretins
jokes.explanation: Frank's inverted logic — that hiring a cretin exonerates him — is a solid absurdist beat with internal consistency. It's funny because it almost sounds like it makes sense for half a second before you realize it's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: So, there's another unrelated diddler in the mix?

jokes.text: Frank has invited the mortician who fixed his face to the pageant — 'Oh, you brought the mortician.' — 'I figure he's a cretin. Why would I have a cretin like that near me if I have something to hide?'
jokes.setup: Mac is alarmed that Frank brought a mortician to a children's pageant
jokes.punchline: Frank's logic — that having a creep near him proves his own innocence — is perfectly backwards. His use of 'cretin' as a neutral descriptor is also funny.
jokes.explanation: Frank's inverted logic ('having a cretin near me proves I have nothing to hide') is the same satirical engine as the entire episode — the gang's attempts to look innocent are always exactly wrong. His casual use of 'cretin' as a simple description is also funny. Character-specific logic.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: It's like throwing a picnic at the beach and getting pissed when the seagulls show up.

jokes.text: Artemis has been hired to work the soundboard and announces she's going to get high before the show
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are stressed about putting on a good show for the inspector
jokes.punchline: Artemis announces her pre-show ritual is getting high — 'Okay. Seems like a bad idea.' / 'Well, don't get high. It's making us look bad.'
jokes.explanation: Functional Artemis character moment — her casual self-destruction fits but isn't particularly clever. The 'it's making us look bad' line is decent (the concern is optics, not competence) but the setup is thin.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: I tell you, children's beauty pageants are an American tradition, but not a proud one.

jokes.text: Frank's pageant MC introduction: 'Which one of these talented entertainers, who I am not attracted to at all, will be the winner? I'm not attracted to any of them, none of them. And that's the way it is.'
jokes.setup: Frank is MCing the pageant and trying to appear legitimate in front of parents and the inspector
jokes.punchline: He repeatedly and explicitly insists he is not attracted to the children — which only makes him sound more suspect — and punctuates it with the authoritative 'That's the way it is.'
jokes.explanation: A great escalation of the 'protesting too much' joke from the opening speech. Frank's repeated denials — 'not attracted to any of them, none of them' — dig the hole deeper with each repetition. The confident news-anchor closer 'and that's the way it is' is an inspired touch. The structure is tight: each sentence makes it worse than the last.

jokes.text: 'Welcome to our legitimate show of kids. Very, very, very nice.' — Frank trying to describe the children performers
jokes.setup: Frank continues his MC duties and tries to frame the event as normal and professional
jokes.punchline: His description 'legitimate show of kids' and the nervous 'very, very, very nice' reveals the strain of trying to sound innocent
jokes.explanation: Extends the cringe of Frank's MC performance. The triple 'very' signals mounting panic beneath the professional veneer. Functions as a bridge gag rather than a standalone moment.

jokes.text: Frank ushering children offstage: 'Wave. Wave good-bye. Go to your dressing room. Go on. Just don't touch... Go to there.' — Kids: 'Bye, Frank!'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to clear the stage while maintaining optics
jokes.punchline: 'Just don't touch...' — a sentence Frank visibly cannot finish, combined with the children warmly saying 'Bye, Frank!' implying they like him, which makes everything worse
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'just don't touch...' is a great cringe beat — the sentence can only end badly, so Frank leaves it unfinished. The children's affectionate 'Bye, Frank!' is funny because it implies a warmth that the optics cannot survive. Good sustained cringe.

jokes.text: Dee coaching Justine in the dressing room: 'Pop your teeth in. Pop your teeth in right now.' — inserting fake teeth into the child
jokes.setup: Dee is preparing Justine for the pageant
jokes.punchline: The child is wearing fake pageant teeth — 'flippers' — a real and deeply unsettling beauty pageant practice, delivered matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: The 'pop your teeth in' detail is taken from the real world of child pageants — the show uses actual disturbing pageant practices for comedy, which earns the dark humor. 'You look fantastic' after inserting fake teeth into a child captures the twisted normalcy of this world.

jokes.text: Mac and Dee's pageant performance: 'Moms stink! P-ew!' — a song about hating moms, performed with children
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee perform their number with the children in the pageant
jokes.punchline: The song is entirely about hating mothers ('moms stink,' 'moms are stupid,' 'I'd like to throw them all in the trash') performed in front of the children's mothers
jokes.explanation: The concept is strong — the gang's self-absorption leading them to perform a song that actively insults the audience — and the execution builds well. Best detail: performing an anti-mom anthem in front of an audience of mothers at a child pageant.

jokes.text: Song lyric: '♪ A big, humongous pain in my vagina ♪'
jokes.setup: The moms-are-terrible song has been escalating in its insults
jokes.punchline: The song drops an unexpected explicit anatomical lyric mid-children's-pageant-performance
jokes.explanation: Shock value escalation that lands mainly on the contrast with the children's pageant setting. The concept is solid but the joke itself is mostly just the word choice — not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Benjamin's patriotism act: 'People of earth, prepare for the future of patriotism.' Then Yankee Doodle Dandy with a remixed drop
jokes.setup: Charlie has promised to 'update' the patriotic song to make it more exciting for a modern audience
jokes.punchline: The 'update' is Benjamin announcing himself as 'the future of patriotism' before a remixed Yankee Doodle Dandy that apparently turns into a rave
jokes.explanation: 'People of earth, prepare for the future of patriotism' is a great absurdist opener for a child pageant act. The Reagan and FDR quote drops mid-Yankee Doodle are unexpected and funny. The rave implication from the post-show discussion adds additional retroactive comedy.

jokes.text: Benjamin follows the Reagan quote with FDR's 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself'
jokes.setup: Reagan quote dropped mid-Yankee Doodle
jokes.punchline: FDR quote immediately follows as if this is a planned medley of presidential history
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the presidential quotes bit. FDR following Reagan creates the impression of a presidential speech medley, which is funnier than a single quote. Slightly diminished returns vs. the Reagan line since the pattern is established.

jokes.text: Post-show discussion: 'Well, someone should have worn a shirt, right? Probably the kid. The kid definitely.'
jokes.setup: Benjamin apparently performed shirtless at a children's pageant
jokes.punchline: The gang calmly reviews this as a fashion decision — the shirt was needed but hey, that's showbiz
jokes.explanation: The understated critique of a shirtless child performance as a wardrobe choice (not a child-protection concern) is good deadpan. 'The kid definitely' as an afterthought correction is a nice rhythm beat.

jokes.text: 'But at a rave, I feel like that would have been awesome.' / 'I know, but the kids make it weird.'
jokes.setup: They're reviewing the apparently rave-like patriotism act
jokes.punchline: Mac gives the rave a positive review; Dennis's objection is only that the children specifically are what made it weird — implying a shirtless rave without kids would have been fine
jokes.explanation: 'The kids make it weird' is an excellent deadpan line — the inversion of normal thinking (kids at a rave being the problem, not the rave itself) is sharp and efficient. Good economy and structure for a quick exchange.

jokes.text: Frank asks the mortician: 'You bang the dead bodies?'
jokes.setup: Frank is chatting casually with the mortician he brought to the pageant
jokes.punchline: Frank's first question for the mortician is blunt necrophilia inquiry, delivered mid-casual-conversation
jokes.explanation: Frank's total lack of social filter applied to the most extreme taboo question is on-brand. The mortician's hesitant 'no' is a good beat. The setup is thin but the deployment is fast and effective.

jokes.text: Frank's speech about being dead: 'If I was dead, you could bang me all you want. Who cares? Dead body's like a piece of trash. Shove as much shit in there as you want.'
jokes.setup: Frank has asked the mortician about necrophilia and gotten a denial
jokes.punchline: Frank elaborates his personal philosophy on what can be done to his corpse, getting progressively more graphic — 'make a stew out of my ass'
jokes.explanation: Frank's profound indifference to what happens to his own body post-death is excellent character writing — it's consistent with his Season 7 'I've lived my life' energy. The escalation ('bang me,' 'fill me up with cream,' 'make a stew out of my ass') is gleefully disgusting. High character integration.

jokes.text: Frank's mic is on during the entire corpse-use speech. 'Is my mic on?' / 'Oh, God.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been delivering his increasingly graphic dead-body speech with a live microphone at a children's pageant
jokes.punchline: He asks 'Is my mic on?' after the entire speech has broadcast to the room — the horror of the situation lands all at once
jokes.explanation: The 'hot mic' structure is a classic but executed cleanly here. The punch is the delayed reveal — asking if the mic is on after the whole speech rather than mid-way, maximizing damage. 'Oh, God.' as the response is perfectly minimal. Great structural choice.

jokes.text: Frank's cover story for the mic incident: 'That was a mistake. The janitor got a hold of the P.A. system. Puerto Rican guy.'
jokes.setup: Frank needs to explain away his mic'd necrophilia speech to the horrified audience
jokes.punchline: His excuse is both racist (blaming a Puerto Rican janitor) and completely implausible — the janitor theory makes no sense
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Puerto Rican guy' as the scapegoat is both horrifying and very Frank — it's casually racist AND makes no contextual sense as an explanation, which is the double-joke. The confidence with which he delivers this ridiculous alibi is peak Frank Reynolds.

jokes.text: Frank continues making it worse: 'You know, kids are great. I love the kids. Not in a sexual way. No, I was married 20 years, and she was a bitch, but she was old, and I never had a problem getting it up with her.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to rehabilitate his image after the hot-mic disaster
jokes.punchline: His proof that he isn't attracted to children is that he could perform sexually with his old, hated wife — adding TMI marriage details to the existing disaster
jokes.explanation: This is Frank's thesis statement as a character. The logic is so specifically Frank: to prove he's not attracted to children, he cites his sexual history with his elderly ex-wife as evidence of normal adult attraction. The 'she was a bitch, but she was old' construction is unhinged and perfect. This is the climax of the 'everything Frank says makes it worse' engine running throughout the episode. High character integration — this only works from Frank.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Is my mic on? Oh, God.' — immediately cuts to his damage control speech
jokes.setup: Frank realizes his entire necrophilia speech has been broadcast
jokes.punchline: His mortified realization — after the entire speech — that he was mic'd is perfect timing
jokes.explanation: The standard 'realized too late the mic was hot' beat — functional but not original. What elevates it is what preceded it and what follows.

jokes.text: Walter, the inspector, is revealed to be an actual predator who infiltrates pageants
jokes.setup: Walter has been the concerned inspector surveilling the gang the entire episode
jokes.punchline: Police reveal Walter is a known predator who targets children's pageants under the guise of child protection — 'Man's a diddler. Sick son of a bitch goes around all these pageants, pretends he's an inspector.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny misdirection/inversion — the person tasked with catching the bad guys IS the bad guy. The structure is excellent: the entire episode has been about the gang's anxiety over Walter's scrutiny, and the reveal recontextualizes everything. The irony of the gang accidentally running legitimate cover for an actual predator is a strong structural payoff.

jokes.text: 'These things are just magnets for those people. It's like throwing a picnic at the beach and getting pissed when the seagulls show up.'
jokes.setup: Police reveal that yet another predator was lurking at their pageant
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers the analogy of seagulls at a beach picnic as a philosophical shrug — the predators are just an environmental hazard of child pageants
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and a strong contender for the best in the series for this type of joke. The seagulls analogy is shockingly apt, perfectly structured, and highly quotable. It reframes something genuinely awful as a matter-of-fact logistical problem using a vivid, homespun image. The comparison is both accurate and completely unhinged in its casual acceptance. Dennis's flat delivery of this insight is pitch-perfect character work. High originality — this specific analogy is inventive and memorable.

jokes.text: Final conclusion: 'Children's beauty pageants are an American tradition, but not a proud one.' / 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: The episode has just resolved with a predator arrested, chaos all around
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers a measured, news-anchor-style final verdict on child pageants, and Dennis agrees with a flat 'Nope'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback closer. The episode started with Frank invoking American tradition to justify child pageants; Mac closes the same loop with the same language but with the addendum 'not a proud one.' Dennis's 'Nope' is perfectly minimal. Good structural bookending.

jokes.text: Final scene: Samantha wins, jumps up screaming 'Yay, I'm the winner!' despite the entire pageant collapsing
jokes.setup: The pageant has ended in total disaster — predator arrested, gang fleeing, chaos everywhere
jokes.punchline: Samantha still gets awarded the crown and celebrates with full genuine joy, indifferent to everything that happened
jokes.explanation: A good button — the show ends on the meanest character winning, which feels both just and deeply wrong. The gang's chaotic exit contrasting with Samantha's triumphant moment is a solid final image. Satisfying closer without being exceptional.

tmdb_overview: Frank finds himself in the child beauty-pageant business and fears that people might think that he's in it for the wrong reasons. Meanwhile, Dee wages war on stage moms, and Mac, Dennis and Charlie think they have found a contestant to back.
